```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.6, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(width = 90)
has_ggplot <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
# The counts in "How this was checked" are read from the source repository at
# build time: the verification matrix (equivalence/verification-matrix/) and
# the stored growth simulation (validation/).
root <- normalizePath(getwd())
while (!file.exists(file.path(root, "DESCRIPTION")) && dirname(root) != root) {
  root <- dirname(root)
}
evidence <- utils::read.csv(file.path(root, "equivalence", "verification-matrix",
                                      "evidence.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
evidence <- evidence[evidence$current, ]
tests_in <- function(file) sum(evidence$location == file)
checks_in <- function(file, item = "") {
  sum(evidence$checks[evidence$location == file & grepl(item, evidence$item, fixed = TRUE)])
}
failed_in <- function(file) sum(evidence$failed[evidence$location == file])
simulation <- utils::read.csv(file.path(root, "validation", "growth-simulation-r3step.csv"),
                              stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
separated <- simulation[simulation$cell != "weak", ]
coverage <- tapply(separated$covered, separated$cell, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
weak_coverage <- mean(simulation$covered[simulation$cell == "weak"], na.rm = TRUE)
```

When the same people are measured repeatedly, a single average trajectory
often hides several kinds of change: some improve, some hold steady, some
decline. A **growth model with classes** finds those kinds from the data. This
vignette is about the growth mixture model, which lets people vary around
their class trajectory, and its multilevel form for people nested in
clusters; it compares it with latent class growth analysis, the model
without that variation, which has its own article,
[Latent class growth analysis](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/trajectory-classes.html)
(including pass/fail, count and ordered outcomes).

## Two models

- **Latent class growth analysis** (Nagin 2005) gives every class its own
  trajectory. Everyone in a class follows that trajectory exactly; anything
  else is noise.
- **The growth mixture model** (Verbeke and Lesaffre 1996; Muthén and Shedden
  1999) also lets people vary *around* their class trajectory: each has their
  own start and rate of change (random intercepts and slopes).

The difference matters. When people vary within their kind, the first model
can only express that variation by adding classes, so it tends to find more
classes than there are (Bauer and Curran 2003). The second model separates
*kinds* of change from *individual* variation.

Both are one call. Persons are the classified units, so `id` names them and
`class_level = "group"` keeps all of a person's measurements in one class;
`random` adds the random effects.

| Role | Argument | Here |
|---|---|---|
| Outcome, measured repeatedly | left of `~` | `score` |
| Time | right of `~` | `wave` |
| Person | `id`, with `class_level = "group"` | `student` |
| Variation around the class trajectory | `random` | `"wave"`: own start and own slope |
| What predicts the class | `membership` | `"motivation"` |

## The data

`growth_scores` is simulated so the answer is known: 300 students tested on up
to seven waves, of three kinds (improving, stable, declining), each student
varying around their kind's trajectory, with motivation predicting the kind.
About 12% of tests were missed, which these models handle without imputation.

```{r data}
library(latents)
head(growth_scores)
```

## How many classes, and which model?

Fit both models for a range of classes and compare them in one table.
`random_covariance = "equal"` gives every class the same random-effect spread,
the usual first choice.

```{r fits}
trajectories <- function(k) {
  mixture_regression(score ~ wave, growth_scores, n_classes = k,
                     id = "student", class_level = "group",
                     n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
}
growth <- function(k) {
  mixture_regression(score ~ wave, growth_scores, n_classes = k,
                     id = "student", class_level = "group", random = "wave",
                     random_covariance = "equal", n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
}
comparison <- compare_models(
  trajectories_3 = trajectories(3), trajectories_4 = trajectories(4),
  trajectories_5 = trajectories(5),
  growth_2 = growth(2), growth_3 = growth(3), growth_4 = growth(4))
comparison
```

The growth mixture model with three classes is preferred, with nearly all
the BIC weight. The trajectory model without random effects keeps improving
as classes are added: five classes are still better than four, though only
three kinds of student exist. That is the over-extraction described above.

```{r comparison-plot, eval = has_ggplot, fig.height = 4}
plot(comparison)
```

For a test rather than a criterion, `enumerate_regressions()` fits a range of
classes and, with `bootstrap`, adds the bootstrap likelihood-ratio test of
each number of classes against one fewer (McLachlan 1987; Nylund, Asparouhov
and Muthén 2007). It refits both models on data simulated from the smaller
one, so it is slow: with 99 replicates per comparison it took about an hour
on these data. It rejects two classes in favour of three (p = 0.01) and keeps
three against four (p = 0.40).

```{r blrt, eval = FALSE}
enumerate_regressions(score ~ wave, growth_scores, n_classes = 1:4,
                      id = "student", class_level = "group", random = "wave",
                      random_covariance = "equal", bootstrap = 99, seed = 1)
```

## The chosen model

Refit it with motivation predicting the class:

```{r chosen}
fit <- mixture_regression(score ~ wave, growth_scores, n_classes = 3,
                          id = "student", class_level = "group",
                          random = "wave", random_covariance = "equal",
                          membership = "motivation", n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
fit
```

Every table is a data frame from `get_results()`; printing shows the columns
people report, while the data frame keeps every column (standard errors,
statistics, exact p-values and bounds).

```{r tables}
get_results(fit, "random")
get_results(fit, "membership")
```

Students start about 4 points apart and change at rates about 0.7 points per
wave apart within each class; those who start higher tend to grow a little
more slowly (a correlation of about -0.25). More motivated students are less
likely to be in the declining class (class 2) or the stable class (class 3)
than in the improving class.

Because the data were simulated, the classes can be checked against the truth:

```{r recovery}
get_results(fit, "recovery", data = growth_scores, truth = "trajectory")
```

## Distal outcomes

Do the classes differ on something measured once per student? `three_step()`
compares class means with the bias-corrected three-step method (Vermunt 2010;
Bakk and Vermunt 2016), which accounts for students being classified with
error. The trajectory model must be fitted without `membership` for this
correction, so motivation is treated here as a distal variable of the
classes from the model without it:

```{r distal}
trajectory_classes <- mixture_regression(score ~ wave, growth_scores,
                                         n_classes = 3, id = "student",
                                         class_level = "group", random = "wave",
                                         random_covariance = "equal",
                                         n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
three_step(trajectory_classes, data = growth_scores, outcome = "motivation",
           contrast = "pairs")
```

## Predictors of the class, in three steps

`membership` estimates the trajectories and the covariate's effect together,
so adding a covariate can move the classes. `r3step()` keeps the classes of a
model fitted without it: each student is assigned to their most likely class,
and a multinomial logistic regression of that assignment on the covariate is
estimated with the classification errors held at the values the model implies
(Vermunt 2010). The covariate must take one value per
student.

```{r r3step}
r3step(trajectory_classes, data = growth_scores, covariates = "motivation")
```

```{r check-r3step, include = FALSE}
slopes <- get_results(trajectory_classes, "coefficients")
slopes <- slopes[slopes$term == "wave", ]
stable <- which.min(abs(slopes$estimate))
improving <- which.max(slopes$estimate)
declining <- which.min(slopes$estimate)
covariate <- r3step(trajectory_classes, growth_scores, "motivation")
covariate <- covariate[covariate$term == "motivation", ]
stopifnot(stable == 3L,
          covariate$estimate[covariate$outcome == sprintf("class_%d", improving)] > 0,
          covariate$estimate[covariate$outcome == sprintf("class_%d", declining)] < 0,
          all(covariate$p_value < 0.001))
```

The coefficients are log odds against the last class, here the stable one.
More motivated students are more likely to be in the improving class and less
likely to be in the declining class than in the stable class. The standard
errors are a sandwich over students by default (`vcov_type = "observed"` gives
the model-based ones). Like every three-step estimator, `r3step()` treats the
classification errors as known; with weakly separated classes its intervals
are too narrow (see *How this was checked*).

## Predicting for new students

`predict()` applies the fitted model to new students. With `newdata`, every
student is treated as new: the class trajectories and the membership logits
come from the fit, and each student is classified from their own scores.
Suppose three students have been tested on the first three waves only:

```{r new-students}
early <- subset(growth_scores, student %in% c(1, 50, 120) & wave <= 2)
early$student <- early$student + 1000  # new students
predict(fit, early, type = "posterior")
```

```{r check-new-students, include = FALSE}
placed <- predict(fit, early, type = "posterior")
class_slopes <- get_results(fit, "coefficients")
class_slopes <- class_slopes[class_slopes$term == "wave", ]
truth <- as.character(early$trajectory[!duplicated(early$student)])
direction <- c(improving = "up", declining = "down")[truth]
fitted_direction <- ifelse(class_slopes$estimate[match(placed$class, class_slopes$class)] > 1,
                           "up", "down")
stopifnot(min(placed$probability) > 0.95, identical(unname(direction), fitted_direction))
```

Three tests are enough to place each of them with a posterior probability
above 0.95, and in the class whose trajectory matches how they were
simulated. The other types give the curves:

- `"class_response"`: every class's trajectory at each row, with the
  student's prior probability of the class from `membership`. The outcome is
  not needed, so the rows can be future waves.
- `"response"`: the trajectories averaged with those prior probabilities.
- `"class_conditional"` and `"conditional"`: the student's own curve,
  adding their predicted random effects to each class trajectory, and its
  average over the posterior probabilities.
- `"random_effects"`: the predicted random effects under every class.

```{r new-students-curves}
future <- data.frame(student = 1001, wave = 3:6, motivation = early$motivation[1])
predict(fit, future, type = "class_response")
predict(fit, early, type = "conditional")
```

Without `newdata`, `predict()` returns the same quantities for the fitted
students.

## Seeing the classes

The trajectory view shows each class's mean trajectory with its confidence
band, a lighter band where 80% of that class's students' own trajectories lie,
and the observed class means at every wave, which should sit on the curves.

```{r trajectories, eval = has_ggplot}
plot(fit)
```

```{r facet, eval = has_ggplot}
plot(fit, facet = TRUE)
```

Individual students, chosen across each class's range of classification
certainty: their observations, their class trajectory (dashed) and their own
predicted trajectory (solid).

```{r individuals, eval = has_ggplot, fig.height = 6.5}
plot(fit, what = "individuals")
```

The coefficients with their intervals and p-values:

```{r coefficients, eval = has_ggplot}
plot(fit, what = "coefficients")
```

Each student's predicted deviation from their class trajectory, with the
model's 95% ellipse:

```{r random, eval = has_ggplot}
plot(fit, what = "random")
```

How confidently each student is classified, one bar per student:

```{r classification, eval = has_ggplot, fig.height = 4.2}
plot(fit, what = "classification")
```

## Students in schools

When the persons are nested in clusters -- students in schools, patients in
clinics -- the clusters may differ in which trajectories their persons
follow. The multilevel growth mixture model (Asparouhov and Muthén 2008;
Vermunt 2003) gives every cluster a group class, and the group class shifts
how probable each trajectory class is for its persons. `cluster` names the
clusters and `n_group_classes` their number of classes; `group_membership`
names cluster-level covariates of the group class. The `growth_schools` data
have 600 students in 40 schools of two (simulated, hidden) types, in which
most students improve or few do, and a school support programme:

```{r schools}
schools <- mixture_regression(score ~ wave, growth_schools, n_classes = 2,
                              id = "student", class_level = "group",
                              random = "wave", random_covariance = "equal",
                              cluster = "school", n_group_classes = 2,
                              group_membership = "programme",
                              n_starts = 4, seed = 1)
schools
```

The schools are the independent units: the likelihood, the standard errors
and the BIC count schools. The group classes' composition, the schools'
classification and the membership logits (the programme makes a school less
likely to be in the second group class):

```{r schools-tables}
get_results(schools, "group_classes")
head(get_results(schools, "clusters"))
get_results(schools, "membership")
```

The trajectory views read the same as for one level, and the classification
view shows how confidently each student is classified:

```{r schools-plots, eval = has_ggplot}
plot(schools)
plot(schools, what = "coefficients")
```

```{r schools-classification, eval = has_ggplot, fig.height = 4.2}
plot(schools, what = "classification")
```

The number of group classes is compared like the number of classes, from one
(the single-level model with schools as the units) upward:

```{r schools-enumerate}
enumerate_regressions(score ~ wave, growth_schools, n_classes = 2,
                      n_group_classes = 1:3, id = "student",
                      class_level = "group", random = "wave",
                      random_covariance = "equal", cluster = "school",
                      n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
```

## Correlated residuals

The random effects make all of a person's measurements correlated to the same
degree. Measurements close in time are often more alike than distant ones: a
good day tends to be followed by another. `residual_correlation` adds a
process to the residuals that is shared by the classes (Proust-Lima,
Philipps and Liquet 2017):

- `"ar"`, a continuous-time autoregressive process, with covariance
  $\sigma^2 e^{-\rho |t - s|}$ between times $t$ and $s$, so the correlation
  decays with the distance in time;
- `"brownian"`, Brownian motion, with covariance $\sigma^2 \min(t, s)$, a
  deviation that wanders and accumulates.

`residual_time` names the time of the process, by default the first numeric
variable of `random` or of the predictors; the times need not be equally
spaced. The data below are simulated: 200 people rated their mood on six
days, following one of two courses (rising or falling), with a random
intercept and day-to-day residuals following an autoregressive process with
correlation 0.6 between consecutive days.

```{r diary}
set.seed(31)
n <- 200
days <- 0:5
kind <- sample(1:2, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.55, 0.45))
diary <- data.frame(person = rep(seq_len(n), each = length(days)),
                    day = rep(days, n))
process <- unlist(lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
  stats::filter(rnorm(length(days), 0, 0.8), 0.6, method = "recursive")
}))
k <- kind[diary$person]
diary$mood <- c(1, 4)[k] + c(0.5, -0.3)[k] * diary$day +
  rnorm(n)[diary$person] + process + rnorm(nrow(diary), 0, 0.5)

mood <- function(correlation) {
  mixture_regression(mood ~ day, diary, n_classes = 2, id = "person",
                     class_level = "group", random = "intercept",
                     random_covariance = "equal", variance = "equal",
                     residual_correlation = correlation, n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
}
independent <- mood("none")
autoregressive <- mood("ar")
brownian <- mood("brownian")
compare_models(independent = independent, autoregressive = autoregressive,
               brownian = brownian)
```

The autoregressive process is preferred by BIC. Its rate $\rho$ and standard
deviation $\sigma$ are reported with the random effects:

```{r diary-random}
get_results(autoregressive, "random")
get_results(independent, "random")
```

```{r check-diary, include = FALSE}
criteria <- BIC(independent, autoregressive, brownian)
stopifnot(which.min(criteria$BIC) == 2L)
variance_of <- function(x) {
  table <- get_results(x, "random")
  table$estimate[table$parameter == "variance" & table$term == "(Intercept)"]
}
stopifnot(variance_of(independent) > variance_of(autoregressive))
```

Without the process, the random intercept absorbs part of the correlation
between days, and its variance is larger. A process the data cannot separate
from the residual variance or the random effects stays on its bound, with a
warning and no standard error; class-specific residual variances
(`variance = "varying"`) make that more likely. `predict()` adds the
process to the conditional predictions of the observed rows, and it needs
`residual_time` in `newdata`.

## Choices and warnings

- **Random effects.** `random = "intercept"` lets students differ in level
  only; `random = "wave"` in level and rate of change. A formula such as
  `~ 0 + wave` gives a random slope without a random intercept.
- **The random-effect spread.** `"equal"` shares it across classes;
  `"varying"` estimates one per class; `"proportional"` shares its shape and
  lets its size differ. `random_diagonal = TRUE` makes the random effects
  uncorrelated.
- **Curved trajectories.** Use `score ~ wave + I(wave^2)` or
  `score ~ splines::ns(wave, df = 3)`.
- **A degenerate covariance.** When the data cannot support a random effect in
  some class (a variance at zero, or two random effects perfectly
  correlated), the fit warns (`latents_random_boundary`), reports no interval
  for that covariance, and marks it as a boundary in the tables and plots.
  Simplify the random effects, or drop them.

## How this was checked

The model's likelihood equals an independently written dense-matrix
likelihood, and the analytic scores equal numerical derivatives; for the
multilevel model too, whose likelihood is checked against a dense sum over
group classes per school, which reduces to the single-level model when the
group classes coincide. Against
`lcmm::hlme()` (Proust-Lima, Philipps and Liquet 2017), on configurations with
one to three classes, shared, proportional and diagonal covariances and
membership covariates, the likelihoods agree at `hlme`'s own estimates and
`mixture_regression()` reaches at least `hlme`'s maximum.

The other features of this article are checked in the same way. The counts
below are read from the package's verification matrix when this article is
built, and count only checks run on the current source.

- **Predictions.** Given `hlme`'s estimates, on new persons and three
  configurations, `predict()` reproduces `lcmm`'s `predictY()`, `predictClass()` and `predictRE()`:
  the class and averaged trajectories to a relative tolerance of
  $10^{-8}$, the posterior probabilities, own curves and random effects to
  $10^{-6}$
  (`r tests_in("equivalence/test-growth-predict-lcmm.R")` tests,
  `r checks_in("equivalence/test-growth-predict-lcmm.R")` checks,
  `r failed_in("equivalence/test-growth-predict-lcmm.R")` failed). The own
  curves are also compared with a dense empirical Bayes computation.
- **Correlated residuals.** The likelihood equals that of `hlme(cor = AR(time))` and `hlme(cor = BM(time))`
  at `hlme`'s estimates to a relative tolerance of $10^{-8}$, with the same
  number of parameters, and `mixture_regression()` reaches the same maximum
  to $10^{-4}$
  (`r tests_in("equivalence/test-growth-correlated-lcmm.R")` tests,
  `r checks_in("equivalence/test-growth-correlated-lcmm.R")` checks,
  `r failed_in("equivalence/test-growth-correlated-lcmm.R")` failed). It
  also equals a likelihood computed from the dense covariance matrix of each
  person's measurements. The coverage of its intervals has not yet been
  studied by simulation.
- **Three-step regression.** The estimates of `r3step()` on a growth mixture equal the maximum of the fixed-error likelihood written out from Vermunt (2010),
  found by a general-purpose optimizer (to a relative tolerance of $10^{-5}$),
  and its observed-information standard
  errors equal those from that optimizer's Hessian (to $10^{-3}$)
  (`r checks_in("tests/equivalence/test-growth-r3step.R", "maximizes")` checks). In
  a predeclared simulation of `r format(max(simulation$replicate), big.mark = ",")` datasets per design
  (`validation/GROWTH_SIMULATION.md`), the 95% intervals for the covariate's
  slope covered the true value in
  `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * min(coverage))` to
  `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * max(coverage))` of the datasets with separated
  classes, and in `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * weak_coverage)` with weakly
  separated classes, where the classification errors are themselves
  uncertain.
